text:
David ran a gloved hand over the damp, rough-hewn stone of the old lighthouse foundation. The air, thick with the brine of the sea and something else – a faint, metallic tang – vibrated with a low, persistent hum. It wasn't the wind, nor the distant drone of a trawler. It felt deeper, resonating in his sternum like a misplaced heartbeat, an echo of some internal tremor the earth itself couldn't quite contain. The Blackwood Bay old-timers spoke of foundations that never truly settled, of the ground here having a memory, a refusal to let things lie buried.

He pulled out his small, waterproof notepad, the pencil feeling strangely heavy, the hum a constant pressure behind his ears. He focused on the faint scorch marks etched into the rock face, half-hidden by tenacious sea-moss. They weren't from a clean fire, not truly. More like an attempt to cauterize something, an effort that had fallen short. Twice, perhaps. The air, or perhaps just his own anxiety, tasted of ozone.

His gaze drifted to the murky water below, where the tide pulled at the wreckage of an old fishing skiff. It had been salvaged from the seabed just last week, yet already, a dark, viscous slime clung to its rotten planks, as if the depths were trying to reclaim it, or perhaps, keep it tethered to some ancient, stubborn secret. A futile struggle, he thought, against something that simply refused to die.
